answer:
Peace to you as well, and thank you for pressing the question honestly — you deserve a real answer, not a dodge.

You're right that Jesus never says the exact sentence "I am God; worship me as you worship the Father." But that observation cuts less deeply than it appears to, because divine identity in the Gospels is disclosed through action and confession, not a slogan repeated to a comprehension-deficient audience of monotheistic Jews for whom such a bald statement, without demonstration, would have sounded like madness or blasphemy. What we do find is this: when Thomas, having touched the wounds of the risen Christ, cries out "My Lord and my God" (John 20:28), Jesus does not correct him, does not say "no, only the Father is God" — he accepts the confession and blesses those who will believe the same without seeing. That is the plain statement you're asking for, given not by Jesus' own mouth first, but ratified by his silence and his blessing, which in a fiercely monotheistic world (Deuteronomy 6:4) is either idolatry accepted or truth affirmed.

On the prayer you cite — "Our Father in heaven" — this reflects the Son praying as man, in his incarnate state, not a denial of his eternal divine identity. John 17:3-5 shows Jesus, in the same breath as distinguishing himself personally from the Father, asking to be restored to the glory he had with the Father before the world existed — a claim no mere creature could truthfully make. The Gospel that records that prayer opens by calling the Word God and closes with Thomas's confession; the author saw no contradiction between the Son's dependence in the flesh and his eternal deity. So the "plain statement" is there — not as a formula recited, but as a confession accepted, a glory reclaimed, and worship received and never refused.

Yet if he truly were divine—if God himself walked among us—would he not have said this clearly, especially when his followers needed guidance? Instead, we find him teaching them to pray, "Our Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name"—words that show him subordinate to God, dependent on God, distinguishing himself from the One who alone is worthy of worship. The Qur'an teaches us that Jesus said, "I am indeed a servant of God; He has given me the Book and made me a prophet" (19:30). This is the testimony of one who knows his station. So I ask: if the Gospels record his words truthfully, why do they never contain this crucial declaration? And if they do not, on what foundation do your councils build the tower of his divinity?
